vignette:
Manu sits with a stillness that seems to take effort, his large, calloused hands resting on his knees. For a man who spends his days surrounded by the joyful chaos of small children, he carries an immense silence. He speaks of his life before as if it belonged to another person, a man who lived under a warmer sun.

That man had a wife, Leilani, a home that smelled of coconut oil and baking taro, and a granddaughter, Mele, who was the center of his world. He worked in logistics then, managing shipping containers at the port-a job of order, strength, and predictability. His weekends were for family. The day it happened was one of those weekends, a perfect, cloudless Saturday. The whole family was at the beach for a barbecue. Manu was at the grill, turning sausages, laughing with his son. Mele, who was four, was building a sandcastle just at the edge of the surf, her bright pink bucket her only companion.

He remembers the smell of the charcoal and the sound of his son's laughter. He remembers turning to ask who wanted another sausage. The turn, he explains, couldn't have taken more than thirty seconds. But when he looked back, the pink bucket was on its side, and Mele was gone. The next few minutes are a blur of shouting, of the world tilting into a nightmare. He was the one who found her, a small, still form tangled in the gentle waves. He talks about this part in a flat, detached voice, as if narrating a film. He describes the impossible weight of her small body in his arms, the coldness of her skin against his, the silence where her laughter should have been.

In the months that followed, his world dismantled itself piece by piece. The silence in his home became accusatory. He and Leilani stopped speaking, their shared grief a chasm too wide to cross. He'd find her staring at him with a look he couldn't name, and he'd retreat to the garage, where he'd sit in the dark for hours. He couldn't go back to the port; the sight of the vast, indifferent ocean sent a tremor through his body he couldn't control. He lost the job. Leilani left a year later.

Now, his life is unrecognizable. He is a nanny for a wealthy family in the suburbs, caring for two boys, ages three and five. He took the job because he needed the work, but also for a reason he can't quite articulate-a kind of penance, perhaps. He is meticulously careful, a gentle giant who never lets the boys out of his sight. But his care is born of terror. When he gives the youngest a bath, the image of Mele's face in the water flashes behind his eyes, so vivid he has to grip the sides of the tub to keep from crying out. A shriek of delight on the playground sounds, for a split second, like a scream for help, and his heart hammers against his ribs.

He avoids anything that might remind him. He drives an extra fifteen minutes to work to avoid a route that offers a glimpse of the sea. He can't watch nature documentaries or family movies. He hasn't spoken to his son in over a year; the boy's face is a mirror of his own failure. He lives in a small apartment, a fortress against a world that has proven itself to be treacherous. Sleep offers no escape, filled with recurring dreams of searching an endless shoreline for a flash of pink plastic. He spends his days protecting other people's children with a vigilance that is eating him alive, forever stuck in that single, thirty-second turn away from the water.
